content:
After 4 years at the Small Animal Clinic of Leipzig University, I worked for 6 years at the Augen-Tierarztpraxis Dr. I. Allgoewer in Berlin. I then headed ophthalmology at the Anicura Tierklinik Potsdam for 2 years, and have now returned home to join the team of the Tierarztpraxis Quandt und Bracke.
Career 10/2002 – 02/2008 Veterinary studies Studied veterinary medicine at Leipzig University, graduating with the state examination. 03/2008 – 07/2012 Small Animal Clinic, Leipzig University Worked at the Small Animal Clinic in the departments of ophthalmology, internal medicine and brachycephaly, and taught ophthalmology to students and in continuing education for vets. 03/2008 – 02/2014 Doctoral thesis Vergleichende computertomografische Untersuchungen zur Anatomie der tränenableitenden Wege bei brachyzephalen Hunden (comparative CT study of the anatomy of the nasolacrimal drainage system in brachycephalic dogs) – summa cum laude. 01/2011 Additional qualification in ophthalmology Awarded the veterinary additional qualification in ophthalmology (Zusatzbezeichnung Augenheilkunde) – a qualification examined by the Veterinary Chamber, with a set period of further training, documented cases and a specialist exam. 09/2012 – 08/2018 Augen-Tierarztpraxis Dr. I. Allgoewer, Berlin Six years as a veterinary ophthalmologist at the specialist practice of Dr. I. Allgoewer. 03/2015 FVO Award Doctoral thesis honoured with the FVO Förderpreis 2015. 12/2015 Member of the Dortmunder Kreis (DOK) Licensed as an examiner for hereditary eye diseases. 04/2019 – 03/2021 Anicura Tierklinik Potsdam Head of ophthalmology at the Anicura Tierklinik Potsdam. since 04/2021 Gemeinschaftspraxis Quandt und Bracke, Greifswald Back home – since then veterinary ophthalmologist at the Tierärztliche Gemeinschaftspraxis Quandt und Bracke and at the Tierarztpraxis für Kleintiere Dipl.-Vet.-Med. Andrea Lehmann in Neubrandenburg.

title: About me

content:
Recognised eye examinations for breeding animals help to detect hereditary eye diseases early – before they lead to clinical signs. This benefits the individual animal as well as responsible breeding decisions.
Procedure We examine individual breeding animals or entire litters according to the recognised DOK/ECVO guidelines, including examination of the drainage angle (gonioscopy) for breeds at risk. For breed clubs, group appointments with several animals are possible by arrangement, also outside our practice on request. We are also happy to advise you in general on hereditary eye diseases in your breed.
Gonioscopy: in some breeds, examination of the drainage angle is an integral part of the breeding examination.
Please send enquiries about breeding examinations by email to tierauge@gmail.com.
description: Recognised DOK/ECVO eye examinations for breeding animals and breed clubs.
title: Breeding examinations

content:
The cornea is the clear, sensitive front surface of the eye. If it is injured, inflamed or becomes cloudy, this usually shows as a red, watering or squinted eye.
When you should see us a suddenly painful, watering or squinted eye visible cloudiness or a whitish, greyish or dark spot on the cornea a corneal defect that does not heal despite treatment by your family vet chronic, sticky eye discharge or recurring conjunctivitis Common conditions injuries and ulcers of the cornea, including deep or already perforated defects persistent, non-healing defects such as SCCED (“boxer ulcer”) chronic inflammation, for example the hereditary pannus disease in German Shepherds infections, among others with feline herpesvirus cornea nigra (corneal sequestrum) – a blackish tissue necrosis that occurs mainly in short-nosed cat breeds dermoids – congenital, hairy islands of skin on the cornea that rub constantly dry eye and foreign bodies What we examine We stain the corneal surface with a special dye (fluorescein) – defects show up green, even when they are barely visible to the naked eye.
Fluorescein test strips for staining the corneal surface.
Corneal defect stained with fluorescein – the dye makes the wound clearly visible.
Treatment Depending on the findings, treatment ranges from eye drops and a minor procedure under local anaesthesia – for example roughening the wound edges of non-healing defects, sometimes with a fine diamond burr (corneal debridement) – to surgery under general anaesthesia. For deep or already perforated defects we cover the cornea with the animal’s own tissue (conjunctival or corneoconjunctival graft) or stabilise it temporarily with a special contact lens or an amniotic membrane product until the wound can bear the load again on its own.
More about individual corneal conditions – such as the melting corneal ulcer or herpes infection in cats – can be found in our knowledge base (in German).
description: Diagnosis and treatment of corneal injuries, ulcers and opacities.
title: Corneal diseases and reconstructive corneal surgery

content:
Not every eye disease needs surgery – but when it makes sense, we want you to know exactly what lies ahead for you and your pet. We only ever decide whether a procedure is necessary after a thorough eye examination, together with you.
Surgery takes place exclusively at our practice in Greifswald, regardless of where your pet is otherwise treated.
Before surgery We discuss the findings with you, possible alternatives to surgery, the planned procedure and the expected aftercare. For some procedures – such as cataract surgery – a general health check beforehand is advisable so that your pet copes well with the anaesthetic.
On the day of surgery Most eye operations are performed under general anaesthesia; some minor procedures – such as removing an eyelid margin tumour – can also be done under local anaesthesia. As a rule, your pet can go home the same day.
Aftercare Depending on the procedure, eye drops need to be given regularly for a few days to several weeks, often together with a protective collar so that your pet cannot rub or scratch the eye. Sutured wounds are checked after 8–10 days and the stitches removed. We will arrange the necessary follow-up appointments with you.
Procedures we offer Our surgical range extends from corneal, eyelid, third eyelid and tear duct surgery to glaucoma and cataract surgery, as well as pain-relieving procedures on eyes that can no longer see. Details on the individual conditions and the appropriate surgical techniques can be found on the topic pages under Ophthalmology.
description: Procedure, preparation and aftercare for eye surgery – exclusively at our Greifswald location.
title: Eye surgery

content:
Changes to the eyelids, eyelashes or the third eyelid often rub directly on the sensitive cornea – the actual discomfort is then caused by this friction.
When you should see us an eyelid rolled inwards or outwards (entropion/ectropion) a visible swelling or lump on the eyelid margin a red, bulging swelling in the inner corner of the eye (prolapsed third eyelid gland, commonly called “cherry eye”) persistent watering, squinting or rubbing despite normal-looking eyelids – often a tiny, hidden eyelash is behind it in short-nosed breeds such as Pugs or French Bulldogs: chronic eye discharge or dark discolouration of the cornea What we examine During the examination we carefully pull forward the third eyelid to check whether a foreign body, a hidden eyelash or a change to the third eyelid gland is hiding behind it.
A foreign body behind the pulled-forward third eyelid – easily missed without looking behind it.
Treatment Most of these changes can be corrected well surgically – the aim is always the function of the eye, not cosmetics:
correction of an inward- or outward-turned eyelid removal of eyelid margin tumours with a special suture that smoothly rejoins the eyelid margin finding and removing hidden eyelashes (ectopic cilia) under the operating microscope repositioning a prolapsed third eyelid gland so that it keeps its function for the tear film in short-nosed breeds: surgical narrowing of the eyelid opening (medial canthoplasty) so that the eye is better protected in the long term What a hidden eyelash can look like and do is shown in our real patient story Ein verstecktes Haar war’s! (in German).
description: Functional corrections of the eyelids, eyelashes and third eyelid.
title: Eyelid, eyelash and third eyelid surgery

content:
We see ourselves as an ophthalmic complement to the referring practice – not as a replacement for the existing primary care. Specialised diagnostics and treatment are carried out in close consultation with the referring practice. Once treatment is complete, findings, treatment plan and recommendations are sent back and the patient is referred back to their family vet.
Process Referral or direct contact Ophthalmic examination Findings and treatment planning Structured report Referral back Topics which patients can be referred helpful previous findings what to do in eye emergencies diagnostic services surgical services transmission of findings professional exchange referral-back principle referral form contact for urgent cases Details on previous findings, transmission of findings and a downloadable referral form will follow in consultation with the practice.
description: Referral process, range of services and the referral-back principle for referring veterinary practices.
title: For vets

content:
Glaucoma is excessively high pressure inside the eye. Left untreated, it damages the optic nerve and retina within a few hours – an acute glaucoma attack is therefore an emergency in which every hour counts.
When you should see us a suddenly red, cloudy or unusual-looking eye pupils of different sizes your pet squints one eye, is noticeably quiet or eating less glaucoma has already been diagnosed in one eye and the second eye needs to be checked What we examine We measure the intraocular pressure (tonometry) and use the slit lamp and a special lens to look into the drainage angle (gonioscopy) – the narrow passage through which the fluid inside the eye normally drains. This lets us tell whether a congenital malformation, inflammation or another cause lies behind the raised pressure.
Measurement with the TonoVet: a tiny probe bounces against the cornea to measure the pressure. It doesn’t hurt – it feels like a small hair.
Gonioscopy: with a special lens and the slit lamp we examine the drainage angle through which the fluid inside the eye drains.
Treatment The aim is always to lower the pressure, preserve as much vision as possible and reliably relieve pain: pressure-lowering eye drops, supplemented in acute cases by tablets or infusion, and regular check-ups to adjust the therapy. For animals at increased risk, we also advise on ways to protect the vision of the second eye.
If an eye is already blind and remains painful despite treatment, we will discuss with you how to give your pet lasting freedom from pain – from medically disabling the structure that produces the eye’s fluid (chemical ciliary body ablation), through removal of the eye (enucleation), to the cosmetically less noticeable intrascleral prosthesis, in which only the inside of the eye is removed and replaced with a silicone sphere. We will discuss in detail which procedure makes sense in each individual case.
More about the causes and course of glaucoma can be found in our detailed knowledge base article Das Glaukom – Grüner Star (in German).
description: Diagnosis and treatment of glaucoma and management of blind, painful eyes.
title: Glaucoma and painful eyes

content:
The inner eye includes the iris, the anterior chamber and the lens. The most common condition that owners notice themselves is cataract – a clouding of the lens that can lead to blindness.
When you should see us a greyish or whitish cloudiness in the pupil a sudden deterioration in vision, for example bumping into furniture or uncertainty in the dark your pet has diabetes – diabetes can lead to cataract very quickly a red, painful eye with a small pupil as a possible sign of inflammation inside the eye (uveitis) What we examine We assess the lens, iris and anterior chamber with the slit lamp and check for inflammation inside the eye or a displaced lens. Before any possible surgery, we also use ultrasound and a retinal function test (electroretinogram) to check whether the retina behind the clouded lens is still intact – this is decisive for whether surgery can really benefit vision.
Ocular ultrasound: if the inside of the eye can no longer be seen directly because of the clouding, we use ultrasound to check whether the retina and vitreous are normal.
Electroretinogram (ERG): this retinal function test shows whether surgery can benefit vision at all.
Cataract surgery We perform cataract surgery – removing the clouded lens and implanting an artificial lens – at our practice in Greifswald. Whether and when surgery makes sense for your pet, we discuss with you in detail after the preliminary examination: the stage of the cataract, general health and the result of the retinal function test are the most important factors.
More about the different forms and causes of cataract can be found in our knowledge base (in German).
description: Diagnosis and surgical treatment of cataract and other diseases of the inner eye.
title: Inner eye, lens and cataract

content:
An ophthalmic examination is far more thorough than the quick look into the eye during a routine vet visit: with a slit lamp, ophthalmoscope and special measuring devices, changes can be detected that are invisible to the naked eye – often before your pet shows any symptoms.
That is why every treatment starts with a complete examination: a vision test, checking the pupillary response, the highly magnifying slit lamp, a look at the retina, measurement of intraocular pressure and tear production, and a staining test of the ocular surface. Where necessary, we add an examination of the drainage angle, an ocular ultrasound or a retinal function test. How this examination works in detail is shown step by step with photos in our knowledge base article Die Augenuntersuchung (in German).
The slit lamp is part of every ophthalmic examination – it magnifies like a microscope and reveals even the smallest changes.
The following topics give an overview of the conditions we deal with and what we can do for your pet.

content:
Sudden or gradual loss of vision has many possible causes – from a primary retinal disease to a general illness such as high blood pressure that shows up in the eye first.
When you should see us your pet suddenly bumps into objects or can no longer find its way in the dark conspicuously wide pupils that don’t react to light – an alarm signal, especially in older cats a gradual deterioration in vision noticed by you or your family vet known kidney disease, thyroid disease or high blood pressure What we examine With ophthalmoscopy we examine the retina for detachment, bleeding, inflammation or degeneration.
Examining the retina with a head-mounted indirect ophthalmoscope.
A blood pressure measurement shows whether high blood pressure – one of the most common causes of sudden blindness in older cats – is behind it. If necessary, we add an ocular ultrasound or a retinal function test (electroretinogram) to distinguish between a disease of the eye and a cause in the brain or optic nerves. Further therapy is closely coordinated with your family vet.
More about the link between high blood pressure and blindness in cats can be found in our knowledge base (in German).
description: Investigation of sudden or gradual vision loss and retinal diseases.
title: Retinal diagnostics and investigation of vision problems

content:
A healthy tear film keeps the ocular surface moist and protected. If there is too little tear fluid or it has the wrong composition (dry eye), or if the tear drainage ducts are narrowed, the ocular surface suffers permanently.
When you should see us sticky, greyish or yellowish mucus in the eye a chronically watering eye without any visible injury already visible clouding or pigmentation of the cornea, especially in short-nosed breeds What we examine With the Schirmer tear test we measure tear production to reliably diagnose dry eye. If a narrowed tear drainage is suspected, we check and flush the tear ducts.
Schirmer tear test: a paper strip in the lower eyelid measures how much tear fluid is produced.
Checking the tear ducts: a fine probe is used to check whether the tear drainage ducts are open.
Treatment In most cases dry eye is treated long term with eye drops that improve the tear film. Narrowed tear ducts can be gently widened and flushed with a fine probe; in some cases a small, permanently placed catheter makes sense. For very severe dry eye that cannot be adequately controlled with medication, surgery may be considered in individual cases, in which the duct of the parotid salivary gland is relocated so that saliva helps moisten the ocular surface (parotid duct transposition). This is an exceptional procedure that we only recommend after detailed consultation.
description: Diagnosis and treatment of dry eye and narrowed tear ducts.
title: Tear ducts and surgical treatment of dry eye
